All of those give you exposure. Not ownership.

You have a claim — backed by a company's solvency, their compliance team, their relationship with regulators, and their terms of service.

That's permission to own. It can be revised, suspended, or revoked.

Mt. Gox customers had balances.
FTX users had balances.

They also had claims, promises, and terms-of-service agreements.

Every single one of them believed "what's mine is mine" — right up until it wasn't.

True ownership has one definition: unilateral control.

You can move it. No approval needed. No review process. No "your account has been flagged."

The moment another party can say no — you don't own it. You're a creditor with a good relationship. For now.

When someone else controls your access, they control your decisions.

You don't need to be threatened directly. You just need to know the door can be closed.

That knowledge is enough to shape behavior. A long leash is still a leash.

Self-custody is where financial sovereignty becomes real.

Not as an ideology. As a practical fact.

You hold the keys → you are the final authority → no institution, government, or terms-of-service update can override that.

That's what "what's mine is mine" actually means.

Bitcoin didn't just create a new asset.

It created the first tool in history that lets an individual hold value with absolute, verifiable, unbreakable sovereignty.

Self-custody isn't paranoia. It isn't technical overkill.

It's the only way that promise keeps itself.
